title: Hitchhikers Guide to the Internet
summary: Offers hints to new network participants on how the direction of the Internet is set, how to find online information, and how to be a good neighbor on the network. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a friendly guide for newcomers. It tells you who makes the rules, where to look things up, and how to be polite online.

questions: what is the hitchhikers guide to the internet
why is rip limited to 15 hops
subtitle: A 1989 newcomer's orientation to the Internet: who runs it, where to find information, and how to avoid causing trouble.

tldr.problem: People connecting a simple IP network to the Internet in 1989 had to learn a lot of unwritten practice (the "oral tradition") about who sets direction, where to get information, and how to be a good neighbor.
tldr.mechanism: The memo is not a tutorial. It gives pointers and hints on the RFC process, the Network Information Center, mailing lists, address allocation, routing protocols, domain names and common BSD Unix networking problems.
tldr.outcome: It defines no standards. It is an Informational snapshot of Internet practice in September 1989, written with a Douglas Adams flavored notice.

facts.label: Growth noted
facts.value: Over 20% per month on some networks

today: RFC 1118 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It is a snapshot of 1989 practice, so details such as the NIC, the IAB membership and the protocols in use reflect that date.

sections.title: Purpose, Audience and the Internet Itself
sections.content:
RFC 1118 is a guide, not a specification: no standards are defined or specified in this memo. Its notice borrows the tone of Douglas Adams, describing itself as unevenly edited and ending with the advice DON'T PANIC. This is a joke in the style of the book, but the practical content that follows is real.

It assumes the reader knows a simple, unconnected IP network, for example a few 4.3 BSD systems on an Ethernet. Its goal is to bring that person to the point where the network can be connected to the Internet with little danger to either. Appendix A lists remedial reading.

The text defines the Internet as the collection of interoperating networks that grew from the ARPANET once a network layer, the Internet Protocol (IP), let local and long-haul networks work together. It names the groups providing services: ISI acting as the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), SRI International running the Network Information Center (NIC), BBN running information services for CSNET and NSFNET, and Merit for NSFNET. Each network has its own operations center, and problems should go first to the operator your campus is directly connected to.
sections.eli5: This is a welcome handbook for people plugging a small group of computers into the big Internet. It points you to the right places so you do not break anything.

sections.title: RFCs, the NIC and Who Sets Direction
sections.content:
The Internet's inner workings are defined by RFCs. Someone writes a document and mails it to Jon Postel, who acts as referee; it is discussed by everyone interested and, if generally accepted, is given a number. Protocols have a standardization state (standard, draft standard, proposed, experimental or historic) and a separate status (required, recommended, elective or not recommended). A Required Standard such as RFC 791 (IP) must be implemented on any Internet host, while RFC 793 (TCP) is a Recommended Standard. Only a few RFCs specify standards; the current list is in RFC 1100, "IAB Official Protocol Standards".

The NIC provides information by network, telephone and mail. The guide shows how to telnet nic.ddn.mil for queries and how to fetch a document such as NETINFO:NUG.DOC by anonymous FTP, and lists mailbox addresses for general help, registration, hostname changes and suggestions. The NSFNET Network Service Center (NNSC) offers newsletters and the Internet Resource Guide.

Mail reflectors, also called mail exploders, resend each message to a subscriber list. To subscribe you append -REQUEST to the mailbox name. Because one reflector sends separate copies across wide area links, a campus can re-reflect locally, or place messages into a notesfile, so only one copy crosses the wide area network.

Technical direction belongs to the Internet Activities Board (IAB), then chaired by Vint Cerf, supported by a Research Task Force and an Engineering Task Force. The memo lists their research groups, technical areas and working groups as they stood in 1989.
sections.eli5: RFCs are the Internet's rule notes, and a few helper offices keep the phone books and answer questions. A small group of experts decides where everything goes next.

sections.title: Getting and Using IP Addresses
sections.content:
Before a local network can join the Internet it must have a unique IP address, which at the time SRI-NIC allocated: you ask Hostmaster for a template, fill it in and mail it back. An IP address is 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers separated by periods, such as 192.17.5.100.

Addresses came in classes. In class A the first octet is the network and the remaining three are the host; class C has three network octets and one host octet; class B splits two and two. Classes D (multicast) and E (experimental) also exist. Class A networks were nearly all allocated, so in practice a site chose between B and C.

Because some gateways could store only about 700 networks of routing information, the guide suggests a campus announce no more than two discrete network numbers, and use subnetting (RFC 950) if it needs more. A mask lets the Internet see one address while the campus sees several. The example advertises the class B network 128.174 to the Internet while using the mask FF.FF.FF.00 inside the campus. Not all systems could subnet: some 4.2BSD systems need extra software, while 4.3BSD subnets as released.

The text also settles an old confusion over the broadcast address. Some machines used all zeros and some all ones; the all-ones format was adopted, and a system that lets you choose should be set to it (explained in RFC 1009 and RFC 1010).
sections.eli5: Every computer on the Internet needs its own street address, and you must ask the address office for yours. Subnetting is like giving one street number to a whole apartment complex and numbering the flats inside.

sections.title: Routing and Its Problems
sections.content:
The memo lists problems the Internet faced. It was designed for about 50 connected networks but was approaching 1000, and the core gateways could not hold much more. Routing algorithms had issues with updating, stability and optimality, and gateways accepted routing information on faith, so a rogue gateway could cripple the Internet. Some parts were congested, with traffic growing in excess of 20% per month on some networks.

Routing is how a network directs a packet from source to destination. Routers mostly look at the destination address in the IP header. If every node knows the whole network, its view is a historical snapshot, which can cause routing loops until the time to live (TTL) expires. Other protocols know only their own area and send everything else to a default gateway.

The protocols in current use are described one by one. Static routing is the most reliable and easiest for a small network or a leaf. RIP uses hop count and treats a count of 16 as infinity, so hosts more than 15 gateways apart cannot communicate; it also ignores link speed. routed -q listens to RIP without broadcasting. Hello (RFC 891) measures delay in milliseconds and was used on the initial NSFNET backbone. GGP (RFC 823) is a distance-vector protocol used by the original core gateways, and the NSFNET backbone used a link-state SPF protocol (RFC 1074). EGP (RFC 904) is a reachability protocol used between autonomous systems.

Gated speaks RIP, EGP and Hello at once and can filter between them, but converting metrics is hard: translating a RIP 16 into an EGP 6 would make everyone think the gateway can reach what is unreachable.
sections.eli5: Routing is picking which road a letter takes. Some road maps are old photographs, so a letter can end up driving in circles until it runs out of time.

sections.title: Names and the Domain System
sections.content:
All routing uses the IP address. Humans prefer names, so a register at the NIC once held a hosts file that machines fetched nightly. That became too labor intensive and bandwidth hungry, so the Domain Name Service (DNS), a distributed database mapping names to addresses, was created and is described in RFC 1034.

An address names a connection on a specific network, while a name is a symbolic representation of a list of addresses; if a machine moves, its addresses change but its name can stay. Domain names are tree structured with the root on the right, as in uxc.cso.uiuc.edu.

A resolver on the user's machine contacts a root name server, then the edu server, then the uiuc server, and so on until it receives a list of addresses for the host. Resolvers and some servers cache information. To get your own domain you need two machines reachable from the Internet to act as name servers, and the biggest problem is that someone must maintain the database.

BIND, the Berkeley Internet Name Domain server, implements a name server for UNIX, comes with 4.3BSD and replaces the /etc/hosts file for lookups. It can also supply mail forwarding for hosts not directly reachable (see RFC 974).
sections.eli5: Names are like contact list entries on your phone and addresses are the real phone numbers. The domain system is the helper who looks up the number when you tap the name.

sections.title: What Was Wrong with Berkeley Unix
sections.content:
Many vendor systems (Ultrix, for example) were still based on BSD 4.2, which worked on small Ethernets but had deficiencies on complicated networks. Most were fixed in BSD 4.3. The guide lists several scenarios.

  • ICMP redirects: BSD 4.2 ignored them, so the gateway sent a redirect for every packet. BSD 4.3 updates its routing table from them.
  • Trailers: never standardized. Short transfers work but long FTP transfers appear to hang. On 4.2 they are a boot option that should be off, and 4.3 negotiates them.
  • Retransmissions: BSD 4.2 retransmitted quickly and often, too aggressive on slow lines. BSD 4.3 does better, and Van Jacobson's algorithm does better still.
  • Time to live: some systems set TTL to 15 because RIP's unreachable value is 16, so packets needing more hops fail.

The memo ends with an appendix of major RFCs, contact points and a short glossary (autonomous system, core gateway, count to infinity, hold down, split horizon, DDN). Its security section says only that there are known security bugs in BSD Unix and some network services, and that the guide does not discuss them.
sections.eli5: The popular computer system had some quirks that made it behave badly on big networks. The guide lists the quirks and tells you which newer version fixed them.
